content: The ACP1 gene encodes an enzyme known as low molecular weight phosphotyrosine protein phosphatase in humans. This enzyme is a member of the phosphotyrosine protein phosphatase family. Its primary function is to act as both an acid phosphatase and a protein tyrosine phosphatase. It achieves this by catalyzing the hydrolysis of protein tyrosine phosphate into protein tyrosine and orthophosphate. Additionally, this enzyme is capable of hydrolyzing orthophosphoric monoesters into alcohol and orthophosphate. The ACP1 gene exhibits genetic polymorphism, meaning it exists in multiple genetic forms. Specifically, there are three common alleles associated with this gene, and these alleles segregate at the corresponding genetic locus. This results in the expression of six distinct phenotypes. Each allele is believed to encode at least two electrophoretically distinct isozymes, referred to as Bf and Bs, which are produced in specific ratios depending on the allele. Furthermore, three transcript variants of this gene have been identified, each encoding a unique isoform of the enzyme. In terms of protein-protein interactions, ACP1 has been demonstrated to interact with EPH receptor A2 and EPH receptor B1, which are members of the Eph receptor family involved in various cellular processes.
